transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-11
Start time (UTC): 16:00
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Daniel Ortega (Head of ML, Lynx), Maya Chen (Infra Eng, Lynx), Aaron Patel (CTO, Lynx), Sofia Ruiz (Compliance, Lynx)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align on pilot (they use the word pilot rather than POC) requirements for Lynx Medical: reserved GPU footprint needed, burst strategy during clinic hours, graceful fallback plans for capacity constraints, and a short benchmark plan to validate latency/throughput/cost targets. Agreed on 4-week pilot timeline with benchmark run in week 2.

Topics covered:
- Success criteria (latency p95, throughput, cost per 1k tokens, quality checks)
- Workload sizing: request patterns, token length distribution, concurrency windows
- Reserved capacity sizing and autoscale/burst policy options
- Fallback strategies (model downgrade, regional failover, rate-limit shaping)
- Benchmarks: harness, test data, measurement metrics, synthetic vs replay
- Timeline and deliverables

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick roll call - I'm Jordan Hayes from Redwood, with Priya and Liam on the SE side. Lynx team?
[00:10] Daniel (Customer): Hey Jordan, Daniel here. Maya, Aaron and Sofia on. Sorry for the late start, clinic backlog this morning.
[00:16] Jordan: No worries, totally get it. Goal for today is to scope the pilot — reserved GPUs, a burst buffer plan, and what success looks like. We'll try to get decisions or at least action owners, yeah?
[00:28] Priya (SE): Quick agenda: success criteria, traffic profile, model sizes, reserved pool sizing, burst/fallback options, then benchmarks and timeline. Is that okay?
[00:35] Daniel: Perfect.
[00:38] [02:15] Maya: To start, our main user flow is live note generation in the clinician UI. Average prompt is around 450 tokens but can spike to 1.2k for long visits. Peak concurrency during rounds is about 120 concurrent requests, sustained for a 45 minute window, then drops. Off-peak is ~8 to 12 concurrent.
[02:45] Aaron: Also important — we have real-time constraints. Target for user-facing microcopy is p95 latency under 350ms, ideally under 250ms. If that can't be done we need clear graceful degradation.
[03:05] Priya: Got it. Couple clarifying q's: current model type you run in-house? And are you open to model variants — e.g., smaller quantized model for fallback?
[03:12] Daniel: We're currently on a managed endpoint from MegaCloud AI using their 13B variant. Moving to Redwood for better cost predictability and dedicated control. Yes we are open to a smaller model for non-critical steps.
[03:27] Liam (SE): When you say 120 concurrency at peak, is that sustained token throughput, or request-per-second? We need the RPS and token-per-request distribution.
[03:35] Maya: It's roughly 45 RPS during peaks, tokens/request average 500, but with those longer visits it's closer to 900-1200 tokens sometimes.
[03:44] Priya: That's helpful. For planning reserved capacity, two levers: number of reserved GPU slots sized for baseline sustained throughput and a burst pool that allows short-term capacity spikes. Bursts can be configured as: reserved + preemptible burst instances or a soft-fallback to a smaller model.
[04:02] [05:18] Jordan: On success criteria — can we capture the top three that would make this pilot a win for you? Latency, cost, and inference quality? Any numbers?
[05:27] Daniel: Latency p95 < 350ms is a must. Cost target is tricky but we want less than current managed spend by at least 20% on a per-session basis. And quality: automated BLEU-like checks probably not useful — we'll use a small human eval set where clinical accuracy is judged.
[05:45] Sofia (Compliance): From a compliance side we need audit logs retained for 12 months, KMS integration for keys, and region controls for PHI. SOC 2 report is required pre-engagement.
[05:58] Priya: We have SOC2 and can do KMS/HSM integrations; audit log retention is configurable in Private deployments. For hosted pilot we can run in a dedicated region and sign an NDA for test data.
[06:12] Maya: Good. For size, are you recommending A100-equivalent or can we use mixed instances?
[06:20] Liam: For the 13B-like model and those token ranges, an A100-80GB equivalent per worker is recommended for stable p95, but if you quantize to 4-bit or use a distilled 7B for fallback you can get similar latency on cheaper GPUs. The reserved pool could be 3 workers to start with, with a burst policy that adds up to 6 workers for short windows.
[06:40] [07:30] Daniel: Three reserved workers — what's the math there?
[07:33] Priya: Rough calc: with your 45 RPS and avg 500 tokens, assuming Redwood's batching + KV cache, a single A100-equivalent worker can handle roughly 18-20 RPS for that token length at p95 targets. So 3 workers gives ~54-60 RPS buffer for baseline. Bursts up to +3 workers for handling spikes to 90+ RPS.
[07:55] Jordan: Important to note batching depends on inter-arrival distribution; your traffic bursts during rounds will increase effective batching which helps throughput but may add small tail latency.
[08:08] [09:45] Aaron: If we reserve 3 and allow bursts to 6, what's the cost delta vs a pure hosted shared option? We want to compare committed pricing vs pay-as-you-go burst.
[09:56] Jordan: We'll send reserved pricing two ways: one with committed monthly slots (cheaper per-hour) plus metered burst, and another with higher reserved capacity but lower burst. Typically pilot uses short-term reserved with burst credits to prove the numbers.
[10:12] [11:30] Maya: On fallback — we prefer graceful model downgrade rather than hard failures. For example, if the burst pool is exhausted, route new requests to a quantized 7B for immediate response, and queue or delay heavy generation jobs like full-visit summarization.
[11:45] Priya: Agreed. Redwood supports policy rules for fallback: (1) downgrade model to smaller variant, (2) region failover, (3) rate-limit non-critical endpoints. We can run canary rules that drop to the fallback at defined thresholds.
[12:05] [13:22] Daniel: Can we prioritize clinician-facing short text over long-form summarization?
[13:28] Priya: Yes, route priorities are supported. Short critical routes get higher priority tokens, less critical batch jobs can be delayed or sent to a queue processed on lower-cost instances.
[13:38] Liam: Also, KV cache will help for repeated context patterns — we can pin common prefixes to reduce token work.
[13:48] [15:00] Sofia: Quick check, encryption in transit and at rest - we need HSM-backed key wrapping. Any constraints from Redwood?
[15:08] Jordan: We integrate with customer KMS/HSMs for private deployments; for hosted pilot we can do customer-managed keys in specific regions. We'll include the security doc in the follow-up.
[15:22] [16:50] Daniel: About benchmarks — what does Redwood want from us in terms of test data? Should we provide production trace or synthetic?
[16:58] Priya: Prefer a replay of anonymized production traces to capture real token distributions. Synthetic tests are useful for stress testing extremes. For quality checks we'll need a small labeled set for human eval.
[17:12] Maya: We can export a sanitized traffic trace for the week of highest concurrency. Need to confirm what fields you need.
[17:20] Priya: Request-id, timestamp, prompt length, response length, and flags for priority routes. Also a few gold-standard prompts with expected clinical outputs for quality scoring.
[17:36] [18:45] Daniel: Timeline? We're hoping to decide on vendor in ~6 weeks.
[18:52] Jordan: Proposed pilot timeline: Week 0 (this week) — SOW and sample data exchange; Week 1 — environment provisioning and reserved pool sizing; Week 2 — benchmark runs and initial quality eval; Week 3 — tuning (quantization, batching), Week 4 — final results and business review. Decision and contract negotiation in week 6. Does that align?
[19:17] Aaron: Yes that aligns with our procurement windows.
[19:20] [20:40] Priya: For the benchmark harness we recommend: 1) traffic replay for 2-hour peak window, 2) tail-latency measurement (p50/p95/p99), 3) cost per 1k tokens measurement with both baseline reserved and burst scenario, 4) quality sampling (human review of ~200 outputs).
[20:58] Jordan: We'll instrument token-level cost and include a cost breakdown per route.
[21:08] [22:30] Maya: A couple of operational questions — autoscale cooldowns and pre-warm time for added workers? If the burst is adding new containers there may be cold-starts.
[22:40] Liam: Right, pre-warm is a concern. Two burst styles: warm standby reserved slots (kept hot but cheaper pricing) versus on-demand cold instances that take ~30-60s to warm. For your user flows that are short-lived spikes, warm standby or preheated micro-workers are better. We can propose a mixed approach: keep one warm standby worker and allow cold scale for extra burst.
[23:10] Daniel: That sounds reasonable. We also need observability: per-route p95 dashboards, token-level cost, and audit logs mapped to request IDs.
[23:26] Jordan: Redwood Console provides per-route latency and cost breakdowns, plus tracing hooks to tie logs to request IDs. We'll include a screenshot of the console in the follow-up.
[23:40] [25:00] Sofia: Regarding data residency — if test data contains PHI we need it to stay in us-east-1 and only stored for the pilot duration (12 months max retention not necessary for pilot).
[25:12] Priya: For pilot we can limit storage retention to 30 days and run in us-east-1; for production we can set 12-month retention. We'll capture the requirement in the SOW.
[25:26] [26:40] Aaron: Any potential vendor lock-in if we adopt Redwood's runtime?
[26:48] Jordan: Client-side integration uses standard REST/SDK calls and model-version pinning. We don't force proprietary model formats; you can export the prompts and model configs. For Private deployment we can even run behind your VPC. So minimal lock-in.
[27:05] [28:22] Daniel: Benchmarks — what's the threshold for passing? Specific numbers?
[28:30] Priya: Suggested pass/fail criteria: p95 latency < 350ms for priority routes; cost per 1k tokens no higher than 80% of your current spend per-session (we'll calculate exact), and human-quality pass rate >= 90% on clinical accuracy for priority prompts. If any single criterion fails we'll propose remediation steps (e.g., quantize, increase reserved slots).
[28:58] [30:00] Maya: On the human eval, how many reviewers and what scoring rubric?
[30:07] Priya: We'll coordinate on a rubric; typical pilot uses 3 clinician reviewers on 200 samples with majority vote and comments for failures.
[30:20] [31:10] Jordan: Pricing model for pilot — two options: low-commit pilot (1-month reserved, metered burst) or short reserved term with slightly discounted reserved rate. We'll include both scenarios in the SOW.
[31:30] Aaron: How do we handle spike-driven cost overruns?
[31:36] Jordan: We can set budget alerts and automatic hard caps that prevent bursts beyond a dollar threshold; also auto-fallback to smaller model when budget thresholds are hit.
[31:48] [33:00] Daniel: Are there any limitations on the private deployment side for KMS integration or air-gap?
[33:08] Priya: Private on-prem has full KMS/HSM support; air-gapped installs are possible but increase setup time. For pilot we recommend dedicated hosted with KMS and audit controls.
[33:22] [34:40] Maya: Any benchmark scripts or ref harness we can run internally to sanity check?
[34:48] Liam: Yes, Priya will share a harness that supports replay, synthetic heavy tails, and quality sampling. It's lightweight — a Docker image and a small config to point at your traces.
[35:00] Priya: I'll also include sample prompting templates and tokenization checks so you can pre-validate that your sanitized traces look right.
[35:12] [36:35] Sophie (typo in transcript - actually Sofia): Sorry, quick - will you provide an NDA or do you need ours?
[36:42] Jordan: We can sign your NDA; we'll also attach Redwood's SOC 2 summary and data handling appendix in the follow-up.
[36:50] [38:10] Daniel: On a more technical note — KV cache effectiveness? Our notes often have repetitive headers and patient metadata that's repeated across requests.
[38:20] Priya: KV caching is useful for repeated prefixes; we can configure prefix caching for session tokens which reduces per-request compute. For long visits with changing contexts we still pay for new tokens, but common sections get cached.
[38:33] [40:05] Aaron: Let's talk fallback in more detail — if the fallback to 7B changes the output behavior meaningfully, how do we surface that risk to clinicians?
[40:16] Priya: Good point. We suggest annotating responses with confidence levels and adding a visible banner in the UI when a fallback model is used for a request. Also flag those sessions for review in a post-run quality audit so clinicians aren't blindsided.
[40:30] [42:00] Maya: For the benchmark run we'll need a stable baseline — are there recommended warm up runs?
[42:08] Liam: Yes, do a 15-minute warm-up at ~50% load before the measured 2-hour run. Capture p50/p95/p99, CPU/GPU utilization, and queue lengths.
[42:22] [44:10] Jordan: Recap of key decisions so far: (1) Pilot = 4 weeks, (2) Reserved starting pool = 3 A100-equivalent workers, burst up to 6, (3) Fallback = quantized 7B + rate-limit non-critical jobs, (4) Benchmarks = replay of sanitized traces + human eval, (5) Compliance = KMS + SOC2 docs to be exchanged.
[44:35] Daniel: That captures it. A couple of follow-ups — we'll send sanitized traces by Tuesday and expect the SOW and pricing by Friday.
[44:46] Jordan: We'll target sending SOW by 2026-10-15, Priya will share the harness earlier, and we'll schedule the benchmark for week of 2026-10-19.
[45:00] [46:20] Sofia: Action for me — I'll run the compliance checklist internally and get back with any blockers.
[46:28] Daniel: Quick question: do you have references in healthcare?
[46:33] Jordan: Yes, we have two anonymized healthcare case studies and a contact at a hospital EHR integrator; we'll share references in the follow-up.
[46:45] [48:00] Maya: What telemetry will we get during the run? Need per-request id links, error rates, and a token-cost estimate in near real time.
[48:10] Liam: The console provides per-route metrics and we can export CSVs with token counts per request; we can stream logs to your SI for near-real-time analysis.
[48:22] [50:00] Aaron: If the pilot passes, what's the path to production?
[50:08] Jordan: Typical path is: expand reserved capacity, migrate production traffic gradually with canaries, set up longer retention for logs and adjust SLA/contract. We'll support a one-month ramp plan and a joint operations review.
[50:20] [51:30] Daniel: Any red flags we should watch for going into the benchmark?
[51:36] Priya: Watch for tokenization mismatches (that can inflate cost), cold-start heavy patterns (we recommend warm standby), and any prompt patterns that generate excessively long outputs. We'll include diagnostics in the harness.
[51:50] [53:00] Jordan: Alright last bit — who will be the single point of contact for procurement and who signs off on the pilot?
[53:08] Aaron: I'll handle procurement and contract review, Daniel will own technical sign-off, and Sofia will approve compliance artifacts.
[53:20] Jordan: Great. We'll create a one-page success matrix and send that with the SOW.
[53:30] [55:00] Daniel: Thanks everyone.
[55:05] Jordan: Thanks all. We'll follow up with SOW, security docs, harness. Expect the SOW by 2026-10-15.
[55:18] Priya: I'll share the benchmark harness and sample config by 2026-10-14.
[55:25] Maya: We'll aim to send sanitized traces by 2026-10-13.
[55:33] Jordan: Perfect. End of call.

References noted in call:

End of transcript.
